roots-1: The backup job is triggered by a cron-style scheduler on a single host rather than a managed backup service.
The job script uses a lock or overlap guard that exits early when a previous run appears active.
Existing alerting reacts to error exit codes or error logs, not to the absence of a completed backup.
No regular restore test or backup-inventory audit is currently scheduled.
1.why.1: The backup is a cron entry on the database host that runs a wrapper shell script; there is no job orchestrator tracking run state.
The existing alert is a failure hook that pages on-call when the wrapper exits nonzero.
Backups are written to a remote storage location such as an object-storage bucket or NFS mount.
1.why.2: The backup is a cron-launched shell wrapper on a single Linux host that runs a dump tool such as pg_dump or mysqldump.
Mutual exclusion uses a hand-rolled lockfile containing a PID rather than kernel-managed flock.
Dump output is written to a network-mounted backup share.
1.why.3: The backup job runs from cron on a single host and writes dump files to object storage.
The backup was set up by one engineer rather than delivered as a team-owned service.
At least one earlier restore already hit a missing backup before this analysis.

inputs.input: Our nightly database backup job silently skips some runs, and nobody notices until a restore is needed.

answers.answer: Alerting fires only on a failed exit code, so a run that never starts or exits early emits no signal at all.
The alert is an on-failure trap inside the backup wrapper script, so it only fires when that script runs and errors.
The backup was set up as a lone cron entry on the database host, with no orchestrator to own run state or alerting.
The monitoring stack collects host metrics only and offers no job-level check, so the script's own trap was the sole hook available.
Guard clauses for an unmounted backup target or full disk log a warning and exit 0, which the failure trap treats as success.
No heartbeat or dead-man's-switch expects a success signal each night, so an absent run looks identical to a quiet night.
The job predates the team's adoption of expected-by-time checks, and nobody retrofitted one when that tooling arrived.
The job writes no completion timestamp or backup size anywhere monitoring reads, so there is no value that could go stale.
The original author moved teams and no one now owns the backup job end to end, so its monitoring was never revisited.
After noisy night pages, the backup alert rules were trimmed to hard failures only, dropping warnings for late or skipped runs.
Transient network blips to the backup storage triggered retry warnings that paged at night, so on-call pushed for fewer backup alerts.
The rule changes were reviewed only for noise reduction, with no check that each failure mode of the job kept alert coverage.
On-call health is measured in pages per week, so deleting alerts looked like progress while missed-backup risk stayed invisible.
A stale lock from an overrunning or crashed previous run makes the next night's job exit cleanly with success, skipping the backup.
The wrapper deliberately treats "lock already held" as a harmless no-op and returns exit 0, to avoid overlapping runs.
The locking snippet was copied from a frequent every-few-minutes job, where skipping one overlapping run costs nothing, unlike a once-nightly backup.
Cron mailed every non-zero exit, so the author made expected overlaps return success to stop nuisance emails.
The scheduler contract offers only success or failure, with no distinct "skipped" status the wrapper could report instead.
The lockfile has no expiry or liveness check, so a crashed run's lock persists until someone deletes it by hand.
Lock removal lives in an EXIT trap, which never runs when the dump is SIGKILLed by the OOM killer or the host reboots.
The script tests only whether the lockfile exists, never whether the PID written inside it is still running.
The lockfile sits on persistent disk rather than tmpfs under /run, so even a reboot does not clear it.
The dump step has no timeout or watchdog, so a hung run keeps holding the lock into the next night's start.
The dump blocks waiting on a table lock held by a long-running transaction or migration left open overnight.
Writes to the backup share stall on an unresponsive hard-mounted NFS export, leaving the dump process blocked indefinitely.
The script dates from when dumps took minutes, and no upper bound was added as database growth stretched runtimes to hours.
No scheduled restore drill or check for tonight's backup file exists, so missing backups are first discovered during a real restore.
No team owns the backup's outcome; the cron script was added by one engineer and never assigned to an on-call rotation.
The engineer who wrote the script moved on, and the handover skipped it because it lived only in crontab, not the service catalog.
Backups sit between the DBA and platform teams, and each assumes the other watches the storage bucket for missing nightly files.
No audit or compliance requirement demands daily evidence of a backup, so management never had reason to name an owner.
Backup success was defined as the cron job completing, so nobody set a recovery objective requiring proof that tonight's file is restorable.
No recovery point or recovery time target was ever agreed with the business, leaving nothing measurable for a drill to check.
Real restores happen only a few times a year, so the missing-file gap stayed invisible between incidents and never gained priority.
The earlier restore postmortem closed its action item as a one-off fix instead of a recurring scheduled drill or file-presence check.
A full restore drill is costly, needing a spare database host and hours of runtime, so it was judged not worth automating.
No staging host has enough disk to hold a restored copy of the production database, so every drill needs provisioning first.
Dump files move to a cold storage tier with retrieval fees and delays, which discourages routinely pulling one back for testing.
The restore procedure is an undocumented manual sequence of commands, so there is no script a scheduler could run unattended.
